title: JSON Schemas & Function Calls — API + Console Walkthrough
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a product walkthrough focused on structured JSON output and function calling. Demo covered API parameters, Console schema upload, guardrails for validation, and Optimize recommendations for batch and caching. Customer had latency/cost tradeoff concerns and asked about private deployment + audit logs. Next steps: send security pack, share demo recording, run a short pilot with a sample schema and 2-week POC pricing.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Tom (Redwood SE), Lin (Product), Nora (Solutions), Maya (Acme Data Eng), Jorge (Acme CTO), Samira (Product), Ethan (Infra)
---
[00:00] Aisha (AE, Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick intro round — we'll run a short demo focused on JSON/schema output and function calling, show the Console config, and then walk through Optimize suggestions for cost and latency. Tom, you want to drive the demo?
[00:18] Tom (SE, Redwood): Yeah happy to. Quick note on flow: we'll start on the API side — how you can request structured JSON via the JSON mode and schemas, then flip to the Console to show route config and guardrails, and finish with Optimize recommendations and how to use model variants / fallback.
[00:34] Maya (Acme): Great — high level we have a ticketing assistant use case, so outputs need to be strict JSON matching our fields (ticket_id, priority, assignee_email). Also we have compliance constraints — everything must stay in our VPC for certain customers.
[00:48] Jorge (CTO, Acme): We care about 99th pct latency being under 600ms for single-threaded requests, and cost per 1k tokens can't go up more than 20% from our current provider.
[01:02] Tom: Understood. We'll show quantization/model variant options and batching tradeoffs. Also show KV cache / prefix caching to reduce repeated token costs.
[01:15] Samira (Prod): Also curious how function calling integrates. We have microservices that need typed payloads; ideally the model emits structured objects we can map directly.
[01:28] Tom: Perfect. I'll start a quick API call from Postman — note this is a recorded demo using a hosted Redwood endpoint. Sending a generation with "mode": "json", attaching an input schema.
[01:45] [typing sounds — demo]
[02:00] Tom: Ok here's the call body: temp 0.0, stream true, mode json, schema: { title: \"ticket\", type: \"object\", properties: { ticket_id: {type: \"string\"}, priority: {enum: [\"low\", \"medium\", \"high\"]}, assignee_email: {type: \"string\", format: \"email\"} }, required: [\"ticket_id\", \"priority\"] } — and we're also setting function_call hint: \"route_to_ticket_service\".
[02:25] Maya: So if the model hallucinated a non-email, would Redwood validate and reject? We need hard guarantees for CI/CD.
[02:34] Tom: There's two layers. First, the runtime enforces schema validation when mode is json — you'll either get a parsed JSON response or an explicit schema error. Second, in the Console you can set guardrails to transform or reject and trigger fallback. We'll show that in a second.
[02:48] Aisha: Note that for dedicated/private customers we can enable even stricter validation hooks and webhook retries so the generator can't slip malformed payloads into downstream services.
[02:59] Ethan (Infra): On private, what's the auth flow? Do we still control keys, or can we integrate KMS/HSM?
[03:08] Lin (Product): For Redwood Private you get a customer-managed control plane and you can bring your own KMS or integrate with cloud KMS. We also keep audit logs and have options to push logs to your S3 or Splunk.
[03:22] [demo continues — showing console]
[03:30] Tom: Flipping to the Console: here's a route config named "ticket-parser-prod". You can upload a JSON schema directly or paste it. We also have a field to attach a function mapping: route_to_ticket_service with the HTTP endpoint and a typed payload mapping.
[03:50] Tom: I'm going to toggle the strict mode — this means any response that doesn't validate will be returned with an error code and won't call the function. If you toggle to repair mode, Redwood will attempt to coerce or call a post-processing hook.
[04:05] Samira: What's the repair rule? Like if priority is \"urgent\" but not in enum, will it map to high?
[04:12] Tom: We have heuristic mapping rules and you can also upload custom correction scripts. Out of the box, there's a small mapping table (urgent -> high, lowish -> low) but for enterprise you can add a transformation lambda that runs inside your VPC.
[04:26] Maya: Can we see a streaming example where the model starts emitting fields and then the function is invoked? We do streaming on the frontend and need partials.
[04:36] Tom: Sure. Here's a streaming invocation with schema. You'll see the stream tokens come in and the JSON parser emits a partial object as it parses. When the parser hits a complete object and validation passes, the function call is triggered. If validation fails at the end, the system returns a schema_error event in the stream.
[04:57] [demo — simulated stream appears]
[05:10] Tom: Notice the stream includes an event: {\"type\":\"schema_partial\", \"payload\": {...}} then final event {\"type\":\"schema_complete\"}.
[05:22] Jorge: Any gotchas for large messages — e.g., long description fields? Will schema enforcement block due to token limits?
[05:31] Tom: The runtime validates parsed JSON, not tokens, so long string fields are fine up to the model limit. For very large fields we recommend setting maxLength and also offloading large blobs to attachments (we support signed URLs in the function payload).
[05:48] Maya: How do we handle retries if the downstream ticket service is 503? We can't double-create tickets.
[05:55] Nora (Solutions): Redwood's function calling supports idempotency keys and will only execute once if you provide a stable key. We also have a retry/backoff policy and can mark retries as safe or unsafe.
[06:07] Ethan: Can we run this in our VPC private deployment and keep the model weights on-prem?
[06:13] Lin: We offer a Private package that can be deployed on customer-managed infra. The control plane can be hosted or self-hosted depending on the contract; for certain regulated customers we do air-gapped installs. Also note the runtime still supports quantized open models to reduce infra footprint.
[06:28] [slight crosstalk — connection noise]
[06:40] Tom: Switching to function design: Best practice is to keep function schemas shallow and typed, include idempotency fields, and avoid embedding large binary blobs inline. We'll show an example mapping into a ticket service endpoint.
[06:57] Tom: Example function signature: route_to_ticket_service(ticket_id string, priority enum, assignee_email string, description string, attachments array[string], idempotency_key string).
[07:10] Maya: On the API side, how do we control fallback to a cheaper model? Sometimes we want to use a smaller model for quick triage and fall back to a stronger model for final extraction.
[07:20] Tom: In the Console you can configure model routing rules on a route: primary model, fallback model(s), and a capacity/cost policy. We do automatic fallback if latency spikes or loss of capacity. Also Optimize will analyze your workload and suggest a mix of models and quantization to hit your cost/latency targets.
[07:39] Samira: Show Optimize quickly?
[07:42] Tom: Sure — Optimize scans token histograms, seq length distribution, and suggests batching settings and whether to enable prefix caching for repeated prompts. Here it recommends: batch_size 8 for background batch work, enable prefix cache for template prompts, quantize to int8 for the smaller model, and keep int16 for the high-accuracy model used in fallback. Estimated savings: ~34% token cost for our sample set.
[08:05] Maya: That sounds promising. Our main concern is accuracy of the structured fields after quantization. Do you track regressions?
[08:14] Lin: Yes — Redwood Optimize ties to evals. You can attach a prompt-eval set and get quality regression alerts if a rollout increases schema errors or lowers extraction F1. We also do shadow runs when you change model variants.
[08:27] Jorge: Security/compliance questions — SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and data residency. Can you give specifics?
[08:36] Aisha: For SSO we support SAML/OIDC, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC groups. Audit logs are immutable and can be exported; for Private installs you can push logs into your SIEM. We have SOC2 Type II and are pursuing ISO certification; I'll send the security pack after the call.
[08:52] Samira: Any mention of third-party vendors in the logs while using hosted? We need to ensure PII never goes to external analytics.
[08:59] Lin: Hosted stores minimal telemetry; customer content retention is configurable. For PII-sensitive workloads we recommend Private with customer-managed logging.
[09:10] [short pause — Tom sets up an error scenario]
[09:20] Tom: Let's force a schema violation — I'll pass priority: \"urgent\" which isn't in the enum, and strict mode ON.
[09:29] [demo]
[09:38] Tom: Response: HTTP 422 schema_error with message \"value not in enum\" and the original candidate in the logs. You'll get an event in the Console with the mismatch and a suggestion to add a mapping.
[09:50] Maya: Good. But in production we prefer repair mode so we don't break UX. How does repair affect downstream idempotency?
[09:57] Nora: When repair is enabled, Redwood will emit a corrected payload and still attach an audit record showing original + repaired versions. Idempotency key remains the same so downstream won't double-create.
[10:10] Ethan: Can the repair step call an internal microservice to verify mappings? We want the mapping logic inside our network.
[10:17] Tom: Yes, you can wire a post-process webhook inside your VPC. That hook can run your mapping service and return a transformed payload.
[10:25] [Customer questions pivot to pricing]
[10:30] Jorge: Pricing — what would a 2-week pilot cost for a modest 100k token trial?
[10:36] Aisha: For a pilot we typically offer a fixed POC pricing or credits. I'll send a proposal; baseline hosted API per token applies but we can do a capped pilot quote.
[10:45] Tom: Also note Dedicated reserved capacity pricing differs; if you commit monthly we can give a predictable per-token cost. Optimize will show the delta between hosted and dedicated in your workload.
[10:56] Maya: Any public benchmarks for structured JSON reliability across models? We care about schema pass rates.
[11:03] Lin: We publish bench charts for common extraction tasks on the docs and can share an internal spreadsheet that shows pass rates per model variant and token distribution. We'll attach that.
[11:12] Samira: Let's talk timeline — we want a POC in June and potential Dedicated in Q3 if it hits targets.
[11:18] Aisha: Sounds doable. We'll aim to provision a pilot env in the next week and run a 2-week pilot in June.
[11:25] [recap and closeout]
[11:26] Aisha: Recap — we'll send security docs, deck & recording; Redwood to provision POC env and run benchmark; Acme to provide sample prompts and success criteria. Next meeting to sync after pilot kickoff.
[11:40] Jorge: Thanks all.
[11:44] Tom: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email.
---
Notes on transcript quality: speaker attribution imperfect in one block (system labelled one of Ethan's interjections as \"Unknown Speaker\"). Some proper nouns garbled e.g., \"KV cash\" appears once in the auto-captions but we confirmed it was KV cache.
